Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$, write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use $0\log0=0$, and set the products $q\log\gamma$ and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$ \int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty, $$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$ \log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu). $$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Define $Q(A)=\int_A q\,d\mu$ and $\Pi(A)=\int_A\pi\,d\mu$. These are probability measures by [F1] and [F7]. If $\Pi(A)=0$, [F4] applied to $\pi\mathbf1_A$ gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. Then [F1] gives $q=0$ almost everywhere on $A$, so $Q(A)=0$ and $Q\ll\Pi$. Define $r=q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and $r=0$ on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $A$, $\int_A r\,d\Pi=\int_{A\cap\{\pi>0\}}q\,d\mu=Q(A)$, so $r=dQ/d\Pi$.

On $\{q>0\}$, $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. The assumed absolute integrability and $\int q\,d\mu=1$ make all terms integrable. Hence $\int\log r\,dQ=\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu=\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)$. This algebraic identity uses the explicit density ratio and no choice axiom.
By [A1] and [F5], the integral $\int\log r\,dQ$ is $D(Q\|\Pi)$ under the library convention. Rearranging step 2.1 gives $\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+D(Q\|\Pi)$.
The measures $Q$ and $\Pi$ are probabilities, so [F6] gives $D(Q\|\Pi)\ge0$. Step 3.1 then yields $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z$.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space

of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$

[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely

$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set

countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let

$$ \int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty, $$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$ \log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu). $$

unspecified statistical model.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

derivations.claim: Fix any admissible replacement $r_j$ and form $u=r_jq_{-j}$. Tonelli [F5] gives $\int u\,d\mu=1$, and the product rectangle formula [F4] gives $\mathbb P_u:=u\mu=\bigotimes_{k=1}^m(u_k\mu_k)$ is the product probability. Each coordinate density $u_k$ is positive and finite almost surely under its factor law; put $X_k=\log u_k(Z_k)$ and $S=\log u(Z)=\sum_{k=1}^mX_k$. By [F1], $\mathbb E_u|S|=\int u|\log u|d\mu<\infty$. Fix $j$ and put $R=\sum_{k\ne j}X_k$, which is finite almost surely under the product of the other factor laws. Since $\{|R|\le n\}$ increases to a full-measure set, choose an integer $K$ for which $p:=\mathbb P_u(|R|\le K)>0$. Product integration from [F5] and [F6] then gives $p\int u_j|\log u_j|d\mu_j=\int_{\{|R|\le K\}}|X_j|\,d\mathbb P_u\le\int|S|d\mathbb P_u+Kp<\infty$, using $|X_j|\le|S|+|R|$ on that event. Thus every factor log is integrable; the same argument applies to the current factor and to $q_j^*$ because their products are admissible.

For each admissible replacement $u_j$, [F1] makes $u\log\gamma$ absolutely integrable. Fubini [F7] applies also to $u|\log\gamma|$, so $\int u_j|h_j|d\mu_j<\infty$ and exchanging the $j$ and $-j$ integrals gives $\int u\log\gamma d\mu=\int u_jh_jd\mu_j$. By step 1.1, all factor log terms are integrable, so $\log u=\log u_j+\log q_{-j}$ almost surely and $\operatorname{ELBO}(u_jq_{-j})=\int u_jh_jd\mu_j-\int u_j\log u_jd\mu_j-\int q_{-j}\log q_{-j}d\mu_{-j}$. The final term is constant over coordinate replacements.

Write $q_j^*=e^{h_j}/c_j$. If $q_j^*=0$, then $h_j=-\infty$ almost everywhere on that set. For any admissible $r_j$, step 2.1 makes $\int r_j|h_j|d\mu_j<\infty$, hence $r_j=0$ almost everywhere there. Thus $r_j\mu_j\ll q_j^*\mu_j$. On $\{q_j^*>0\}$ the ratio $r_j/q_j^*$ is measurable, and for every measurable $A$, $\int_A(r_j/q_j^*)d(q_j^*\mu_j)=\int_{A\cap\{q_j^*>0\}}r_jd\mu_j=\int_Ar_jd\mu_j$, so it is the Radon–Nikodym density.

By [A1] and [F8], $D(r_j\mu_j\|q_j^*\mu_j)=\int r_j\log(r_j/q_j^*)d\mu_j=\int r_j\log r_jd\mu_j-\int r_jh_jd\mu_j+\log c_j$. All terms are finite by step 1.1 and step 2.1. Also $\int q_j^*h_j-\int q_j^*\log q_j^*=\log c_j$. Subtracting the ELBO expressions in step 2.1 therefore gives $\operatorname{ELBO}(q_j^*q_{-j})-\operatorname{ELBO}(r_jq_{-j})=D(r_j\mu_j\|q_j^*\mu_j)\ge0$ by [F9]. The current factor $q_j$ is itself an admissible replacement. Taking $r_j=q_j$ in step 3.2 proves that the update does not decrease ELBO.

$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$

This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$, write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use $0\log0=0$, and set the products $q\log\gamma$ and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

**Inputs:** A finite number $m\ge1$ of sigma-finite factor reference spaces $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$, their product reference measure $\mu$, a measurable target $\gamma$ with finite positive normalizer, an admissible initial mean-field density $q=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j$, and a finite sweep count $N\ge0$.

**Output:** The current admissible product density after at most $N$ full sweeps, together with a status indicating whether the requested sweeps completed or a coordinate update was unavailable.

For each sweep $t=1,\ldots,N$, visit coordinates in the fixed order $j=1,\ldots,m$. At coordinate $j$, keep $q_{-j}:=\prod_{k\ne j}q_k$ fixed; for $m=1$, the empty product reference space is a singleton with unit measure $\mu_{-j}$ and its density is $1$. Form the conditional log expectation
$$h_j(z_j):=\int_{\prod_{k\ne j}\Omega_k}\log\gamma(z_j,z_{-j})q_{-j}(z_{-j})\,d\mu_{-j}(z_{-j}).$$
Use this signed integral only when it is defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity and has a measurable extended-real version; require it to be finite for current $q_j$-almost every $z_j$. Set
$$c_j:=\int_{\Omega_j}e^{h_j(z_j)}\,\mu_j(dz_j).$$
If $0<c_j<\infty$ and the normalized density $q_j^*(z_j):=e^{h_j(z_j)}/c_j$ makes $q_j^*q_{-j}$ an admissible member of the mean-field family, replace $q_j$ by $q_j^*$. Otherwise stop and return the current density with status “coordinate update unavailable.”

The algorithm performs only the requested finite sweeps. It makes no convergence, stationary-point, global-optimum, calibration, or approximation-error claim. A separate theorem on this page proves exact coordinate monotonicity under these conditions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.
